title: What an OS does, kernel vs user mode, system calls
scopeHtml:
Scope: OS roles, privilege modes, syscall mechanism and cost, strace, interrupts, reading CPU time split in top.

Scope: OS roles, privilege modes, syscall mechanism and cost, strace, interrupts, reading CPU time split in top.

notes.title: What an operating system does
notes.html:
An operating system (OS) is the program that shares the machine between all other programs and hides the ugly hardware details. Without it every app would have to talk to the disk controller, the network card and the timer chip itself, and one buggy app could overwrite another's memory.

The OS does four jobs:

  1. Share the CPU between many programs (scheduling).
  2. Share and protect memory (each process gets its own private address space).
  3. Hide devices behind simple ideas: files, sockets, processes.
  4. Enforce rules (who may read which file, who may kill which process).

Worked example. Your Android app calls File.readText(). That becomes read() in libc, which traps into the Linux kernel, which finds the page in the page cache (about 100 ns) or asks the SSD (about 100 microseconds). Your code never knew which one happened. That ignorance is the whole point.

Industry examples. Linux runs nearly all servers, and Android is a Linux kernel plus Java/Kotlin runtime (ART). Containers (Docker, Kubernetes) are not tiny VMs: they are ordinary Linux processes with namespaces and cgroups, so understanding the OS is understanding containers.

Everyday analogy. A building manager: tenants (apps) get their own flats, share the lift and water, and cannot enter each other's flats. They ask the manager for anything shared.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the OS "is" the GUI. The kernel is the core; shells, libc and desktops are outside it.
  • Forgetting that containers share the host kernel (a kernel bug affects all of them).

notes.title: Kernel mode vs user mode
notes.html:
The CPU has privilege levels. User mode can only run safe instructions; kernel mode can do anything. On x86 these are ring 3 (user) and ring 0 (kernel). ARM calls them EL0 and EL1.

Why: if any app could execute "disable interrupts" or "write to any physical address", one bug would freeze the machine. The hardware refuses privileged instructions in user mode and raises an exception instead.

What is privileged: talking to I/O ports and devices, changing page tables, halting the CPU, setting the timer, touching kernel memory.

Kernel memory sits in the same virtual address space (upper half on 64-bit Linux), but pages are marked "supervisor only", so user code that touches them gets a fault (SIGSEGV). After the Meltdown bug (2018) Linux added KPTI: separate page tables for user and kernel, which makes each mode switch more costly (a TLB effect, see the virtual memory note).

Decision gravity. Monolithic kernel (Linux) puts drivers, file systems and networking in kernel mode: fastest, but a driver bug crashes everything. Microkernel (QNX, seL4, MINIX) moves them to user processes: safer, slower due to message passing. Chosen by Linux for speed; switching is a one-way door at OS design time. Hybrid designs (Windows NT, macOS XNU) sit between.

Everyday analogy. A bank: customers stay in the lobby (user mode); only staff go into the vault (kernel mode), and only through a controlled door (the system call).

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing "kernel mode" with "root user". Root is a permission level inside user mode; it still needs system calls.
  • Thinking the kernel is a separate running process. It is code that runs on behalf of processes (and in its own kernel threads).

notes.title: System calls
notes.html:
A system call (syscall) is a request from a program to the kernel: "open this file", "send these bytes", "create a process". It is the only way user code can get kernel services.

Mechanism on x86-64 Linux:

  1. Put the syscall number in rax (for example read = 0, write = 1, openat = 257) and arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9.
  2. Execute the syscall instruction. The CPU switches to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel entry point.
  3. The kernel validates arguments (never trust user pointers), does the work, puts the result in rax (negative values are -errno).
  4. sysret returns to user mode. libc turns the negative result into -1 plus errno.

Common syscalls to know: read/write, openat/close, mmap/munmap/brk, clone/fork/execve/wait4, socket/connect/accept/sendto/recvfrom, epoll_wait, futex, ioctl.

// Same thing, no libc wrapper: write "hi\n" to stdout
syscall(SYS_write, 1, "hi\n", 3);

Industry examples. Go's runtime and Java's JVM both call these through libc or direct syscalls. gVisor (Google) intercepts syscalls from containers and reimplements them in user space for sandboxing: stronger isolation at the price of speed.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant order slip: you cannot walk into the kitchen; you write a numbered order (syscall number, arguments), hand it over, and wait for the dish.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up library function and syscall: printf is libc (buffers in user space); write is the syscall. Buffering is why printf is cheaper per call.
  • Believing malloc is a syscall. It usually is not; it calls brk/mmap only when it needs more memory.

notes.title: Cost of a system call
notes.html:
A syscall is cheap compared with disk, expensive compared with a function call. A plain function call is about 1 to 5 ns. A trivial syscall like getppid costs roughly 100 to 300 ns on modern hardware (more with mitigations such as KPTI/retpoline: figures vary by CPU and kernel, so measure on your box).

Where the cost comes from: mode switch, saving registers, argument checks, cache and TLB disturbance, plus the real work (a read from a socket may take microseconds).

Worked example. Copying a 1 GB file with 1-byte read/write pairs: 2 billion syscalls x 200 ns = 400 s of pure overhead. With a 64 KB buffer: 32,768 syscalls = about 7 ms. That is why every language wraps files in buffered streams (BufferedInputStream, BufferedReader).

Ways production systems cut syscall cost:

  • Batching: writev, sendmmsg, bigger buffers.
  • vDSO: gettimeofday/clock_gettime run in user space by reading a kernel-mapped page, no mode switch (about 20 ns).
  • epoll: one epoll_wait returns many ready sockets instead of one poll per socket.
  • io_uring (Linux 5.1+): shared submission and completion ring buffers; many I/O operations with few or zero syscalls. Used by newer databases and proxies; has had security issues, so some container platforms disable it.
  • Kernel bypass (DPDK, RDMA): skip the kernel for the network path entirely; used in trading and some cloud networks.

Everyday analogy. Carrying shopping upstairs one item per trip versus one bag per trip. The stairs (mode switch) cost the same each time.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising syscalls before profiling. Check strace -c or perf first.
  • Saying all syscalls cost the same. getpid is tiny; fsync can take milliseconds.

notes.title: Watching syscalls with strace
notes.html:
strace prints every syscall a process makes, with arguments, result and time. It uses ptrace, which stops the process at each syscall, so it can slow the target 10x to 100x. Use it on a dev box, or with a narrow filter, or prefer perf trace / eBPF (bpftrace, bcc) in production.

# Run a command under strace
strace -f -tt -T -e trace=openat,read,write cat /etc/hostname

# Attach to a live process (needs permission), follow threads
sudo strace -f -p 4121

# Summary: which syscalls, how many, how much time
strace -c -f ./myapp

Flags: -f follow children and threads, -tt wall-clock timestamps, -T time spent inside each call, -e trace=... filter, -o file write to a file.

Sample output:

$ strace -T -e trace=openat,read,write cat /etc/hostname
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY) = 3 <0.000021>
read(3, "web-01\n", 131072)             = 7 <0.000010>
write(1, "web-01\n", 7)                 = 7 <0.000018>
read(3, "", 131072)                     = 0 <0.000006>

$ strace -c ls > /dev/null
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
 38.10    0.000064          5        12           mmap
 21.43    0.000036          6         6           openat
  ...

Reading it: = 3 is a file descriptor, = 0 on read is end of file, = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory) is a failure. Classic findings: a startup that does hundreds of failed openat on missing config paths, a loop doing futex waits (lock contention), a process stuck in epoll_wait (idle, healthy) versus stuck in read on a socket (waiting on a peer).

Production incident pattern. Service latency jumps; CPU is low. strace -f -T -p PID shows connect(...) = 0 <2.003>: each DNS or connect call takes 2 s. The metric to confirm is the p99 of upstream call time. Fix the resolver, not the app.

Everyday analogy. A flight recorder for a program's requests to the kernel.

Common interview traps.

  • Running strace -p on a latency-critical production process and causing the outage you wanted to debug.
  • Forgetting -f: you attach to the main thread of a multi-threaded JVM and see only futex.

notes.title: Interrupts, traps and exceptions
notes.html:
Besides syscalls, the CPU enters the kernel for two other reasons: hardware interrupts and faults.

  • Interrupt (asynchronous): a device says "I need attention". Timer tick, NIC received a packet, disk finished. The CPU pauses user code, runs the interrupt handler, then resumes.
  • Exception/fault (synchronous): the running instruction did something that needs the kernel: page fault (see the virtual memory note), divide by zero, illegal instruction.
  • Trap: deliberate, such as the syscall instruction or a breakpoint.

The timer interrupt is how the OS regains control from a program stuck in while(true){}: every 1 to 10 ms (CONFIG_HZ, often 250 or 1000) the kernel can decide to switch to another process. This is called preemption.

Modern kernels split interrupt work: a short top half acknowledges the device, a bottom half (softirq, tasklet, NAPI) does the rest. You see it in top as si (softirq) CPU time. A busy NIC can pin one core at 100% si; fix with RSS/multiple queues, irqbalance, or RPS.

# Which CPUs service which interrupts
cat /proc/interrupts | head
# Cumulative counts of interrupts and context switches
grep -E 'intr|ctxt' /proc/stat

Everyday analogy. You are reading (user code). A doorbell ring (interrupt) makes you pause and answer, then go back to the page. Asking the librarian for a book (syscall) is you choosing to leave your seat.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying only syscalls enter the kernel.
  • Not knowing why a long loop cannot hang the machine: timer interrupt plus preemption.

notes.title: Reading the CPU time split in top
notes.html:
Tying it together: top and vmstat show how CPU time divides between user mode, kernel mode and waiting.

$ top -bn1 | head -5
top - 10:02:11 up 12 days,  3:41,  1 user,  load average: 1.20, 0.90, 0.75
Tasks: 212 total,   1 running, 211 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
%Cpu(s): 12.1 us,  6.3 sy,  0.0 ni, 78.9 id,  2.3 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.4 si,  0.0 st
  • us user mode, sy kernel mode (syscalls, page faults, networking), ni niced user, id idle, wa waiting on I/O, hi/si hardware/software interrupts, st stolen by the hypervisor (noisy neighbour in a VM).

Rules of thumb: high us means your code is busy; high sy (say above 30%) means syscalls, lock contention, context switching or network stack work: run strace -c or perf top. High wa means CPUs are idle only because tasks wait on disk. High st on a cloud VM means resize or move the instance.

vmstat 1 3   # columns: r b | us sy id wa st | in cs

in is interrupts per second, cs context switches per second: sudden growth hints at overload or thread thrash.

Everyday analogy. A kitchen timesheet: cooking (user), talking to suppliers (kernel), waiting for a delivery (wa), standing idle (id).

Common interview traps.

  • Reading wa as "CPU busy". It is idle CPU with outstanding I/O.
  • Ignoring st on cloud instances.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• The OS shares CPU, memory and devices between programs and protects them from each other.
  • User mode is restricted; kernel mode is privileged. The only controlled entry points are syscalls, interrupts and faults.
  • A syscall = number in a register + syscall instruction + kernel work + return. libc wraps it and sets errno.
  • Syscalls cost roughly 100 to 300 ns plus the real work, so batch (buffers, writev, epoll, io_uring) and use the vDSO for time.
  • strace -f -T -c shows which calls are slow, failing or frequent; it is slow itself, so be careful in production, and prefer perf trace or eBPF.
  • Timer interrupts make preemption possible; top splits CPU time into us, sy, wa, si, st and each tells you where to look.
  • Monolithic vs microkernel is a classic speed vs isolation trade-off; containers share one kernel.

questions.subtopic: Role of the OS and containers
questions.promptHtml: What does an operating system actually do for your application, and is a Docker container a small virtual machine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you see the OS as a resource-sharing and protection layer, and whether you understand that containers share the host kernel.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The OS shares the CPU, memory and devices between programs and protects them from each other. It gives each process a private address space, hides disks and NICs behind files and sockets, and enforces permissions. A container is not a VM: it is an ordinary Linux process with namespaces and cgroups, so it shares the host kernel. A VM has its own kernel on virtual hardware.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Four jobs: schedule the CPU, isolate and share memory, abstract devices, enforce access rules. Your app calls read(); it never knows whether the bytes came from the page cache (about 100 ns) or the SSD (about 100 microseconds).

VM:         app -> guest kernel -> hypervisor -> hardware   (own kernel per VM)
Container:  app -> HOST kernel (namespaces + cgroups) -> hardware

Namespaces limit what a process can see (PIDs, mounts, network). cgroups limit what it can use (CPU, memory, pids). Neither creates a new kernel, so a kernel exploit in one container is an exploit of the host.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the OS is the GUI or the shell. The kernel is the core; libc, shells and desktops sit outside it.
  • Saying containers are lighter VMs and missing the shared-kernel security consequence.
  • Believing a container can run a different kernel version than the host.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do containers start in milliseconds and VMs in seconds? -> No guest kernel boot, just process creation plus namespace setup.
  2. How do you harden multi-tenant containers? -> seccomp filters, dropping capabilities, user namespaces, or a syscall-intercepting sandbox like gVisor or a microVM like Firecracker.
  3. Can a container see the host's processes? -> Not by default (PID namespace), but --pid=host removes that wall, which is a common misconfiguration.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists "manages memory and processes". The senior ties it to a consequence: shared kernel means shared blast radius, kernel upgrades hit every container on the node, and tenant isolation needs more than namespaces.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A node kernel panic from a driver bug took down every pod on the node at once, which surprised a team that thought pods were isolated like VMs.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode, and is a process running as root in kernel mode?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A classic fundamentals check that separates hardware privilege from file permissions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The CPU has privilege levels: ring 3 for user code, ring 0 for the kernel on x86. User mode cannot run privileged instructions like touching device ports, changing page tables or halting the CPU. Root is not kernel mode. Root is a permission level inside the OS; a root process still runs in user mode and must ask the kernel through system calls.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Privileged instructions in user mode raise an exception, and the kernel typically kills the process with a signal. The only legal doors into ring 0 are syscalls, interrupts and faults.

On 64-bit Linux the kernel is mapped in the upper half of every process's address space, but its pages are marked supervisor-only. A user access gives a fault and SIGSEGV. After Meltdown (2018), KPTI keeps separate page tables for user and kernel, which makes each transition more expensive because of TLB effects.

ring 3: your code, libc, root-owned daemons
-------------------- syscall / interrupt / fault ---------------
ring 0: kernel, drivers, interrupt handlers

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating root with kernel mode.
  • Thinking the kernel is a separate process. It runs on behalf of the calling process, plus its own kernel threads.
  • Forgetting that loadable kernel modules and drivers run in ring 0 and can crash the machine.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens if user code executes hlt? -> The CPU raises a general protection fault and the kernel sends a fatal signal.
  2. Monolithic vs microkernel? -> Monolithic (Linux) puts drivers and file systems in ring 0 for speed; microkernels (seL4, QNX) move them to user processes for fault isolation at the cost of IPC.
  3. What does KPTI cost? -> Extra page table switches and TLB pressure on every transition; syscall-heavy workloads saw measurable slowdowns (verify on your CPU, PCID reduces it).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "kernel mode has more privileges". Senior: hardware-enforced mechanism, the sole entry points, root being orthogonal, and the cost side effects of mitigations like KPTI.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky third-party kernel driver module panicked hosts under load; the team learned drivers share the kernel's fate, which is why they later preferred user-space alternatives.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what happens when your program calls read(fd, buf, n).

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can trace the user to kernel boundary instead of treating I/O as magic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: read is a libc wrapper. It puts the syscall number in rax and arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, then executes the syscall instruction. The CPU switches to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel entry. The kernel validates the fd and the user pointer, looks in the page cache, and if the data is missing it blocks the task and asks the disk. It copies bytes to my buffer, puts the result in rax, and sysret returns to user mode. libc converts a negative result into -1 plus errno.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App -> libc read() -> syscall insn -> ring 0 entry -> sys_read
    -> fd table lookup -> VFS -> page cache hit? -> copy_to_user -> sysret
                                   miss -> block task, schedule others, wake on I/O completion
  • The kernel never trusts user pointers. It uses copy_to_user, which handles bad addresses by returning EFAULT rather than crashing.
  • A blocked task leaves the run queue; the CPU runs someone else. When the disk interrupt fires, the task becomes runnable again.
  • read may return fewer bytes than asked. Short reads are normal on sockets and pipes.
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
if (n < 0) { /* errno: EINTR, EAGAIN, EBADF ... */ }
else if (n == 0) { /* end of file */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming read fills the whole buffer.
  • Confusing libc functions (printf, fread, which buffer) with syscalls (write, read).
  • Believing malloc is a syscall; it only calls brk or mmap when it needs more memory.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does a return of 0 mean? -> End of file (or a closed peer on a socket).
  2. What is EINTR? -> A signal arrived while blocked; retry unless SA_RESTART applies.
  3. How would you see it live? -> strace -T -e trace=read,openat -p PID, with care in production.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it goes to the kernel and returns data". Senior: registers, validation, page cache hit vs miss, task blocking and wake-up, short reads, errno handling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A client that ignored short reads on TCP parsed half a message and corrupted state under load, but passed all tests on localhost where reads returned full buffers.

questions.contextHtml:
A nightly job copies 1 GB files between volumes. After a rewrite from a shell cp to an in-house tool, the copy takes 8 minutes instead of 4 seconds. CPU shows 100% on one core, mostly system time. strace -c on a 10 MB sample:

% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
 52.10    2.100000           0  10485760           read
 47.50    1.915000           0  10485760           write

The code:

Languages: C++, Java, Kotlin, Python

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
char c;
while (read(in, &c, 1) == 1) write(out, &c, 1);
int b;
while ((b = in.read()) != -1) out.write(b);   // in/out are raw FileInputStream/FileOutputStream
while (true) { val b = input.read(); if (b == -1) break; output.write(b) }  // raw file streams
while (b := f_in.read(1)):      # f_in opened with buffering=0
    f_out.write(b)

Disk throughput is fine (iostat shows 5% util). A colleague suggests a faster SSD.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you prove it, and how much faster can you get?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disk is slow, buy NVMe" or "rewrite in C". Both ignore that CPU is pegged in sy and the strace call count is 20 million for 10 MB.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are streams buffered? (Tells me whether libc/JVM batching exists.) What is the kernel and mitigation state? (Syscall base cost.) Is the file in page cache? (Rules disk out.) Is it one thread?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fall back to cp or sendfile for the nightly run while fixing the tool.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one syscall per byte; (b) disk slow; (c) page cache cold; (d) container seccomp adds per-syscall cost.
  4. How I'd verify each: strace -c shows 10.4 M calls for 10 MB, one per byte. iostat -x 1 shows low util, vmstat shows sy high and wa low, ruling out disk. 2 calls x 1 G x about 200 ns is roughly 400 s, matching the 8 minutes.
  5. Root cause: Every byte pays a mode switch, register save, fd lookup and argument validation. The syscall cost (about 100 to 300 ns) dwarfs the useful work of copying one byte.
  6. Fix: Short-term: use 64 KB to 1 MB buffers (about 16k calls per GB, milliseconds of overhead). Long-term: copy_file_range or sendfile so bytes never reach user space, or ioctl(FICLONE) on reflink file systems.
std::vector<char> buf(1 << 20);
ssize_t n;
while ((n = read(in, buf.data(), buf.size())) > 0) {
    for (ssize_t off = 0; off < n; ) { ssize_t w = write(out, buf.data()+off, n-off); if (w < 0) die(); off += w; }
}
  1. Prevention: Lint rule against unbuffered file streams, a perf test that asserts syscalls per MB, strace -c in CI smoke checks.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not buy hardware (the bottleneck was CPU in the kernel boundary). Not use a gigantic buffer without limit (memory) or ignore partial write.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would mmap be faster? -> It avoids a copy but incurs page faults; for one sequential pass read with a big buffer or copy_file_range is as good and simpler.
  • Why was the 4-second cp so fast? -> Large reads (128 KB) and often copy_file_range; the work is bounded by memory/disk bandwidth.
  • What if the buffer is 4 KB? -> 262k syscalls per GB, still cheap (tens of ms); gains flatten after tens of KB.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A log shipper wrote each line with a separate write to a pipe; at 200k lines/s it burned two cores in sy. Batching into 64 KB writes cut CPU by 90% with no loss of freshness once a 100 ms flush timer was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames disk or hardware.
  • Hire: spots per-byte syscalls and buffers the I/O, citing strace -c.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the overhead, mentions copy_file_range or sendfile, partial writes, and a CI guard.

questions.promptHtml: Besides system calls, how else does the CPU enter the kernel? And how can the OS take the CPU back from a program stuck in while(true){}?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of preemption and the three doors into ring 0.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Three doors: syscalls (deliberate traps), hardware interrupts (a device or timer says "attend to me", asynchronous), and exceptions or faults (the current instruction needs the kernel, like a page fault or divide by zero, synchronous). The timer interrupt fires every 1 to 10 ms, the kernel runs, sees the task has used its slice and switches to another. That preemption is why one infinite loop cannot hang the machine.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Interrupt: asynchronous, unrelated to the current instruction. Handlers are split: a short top half acknowledges the device with interrupts masked briefly; the bottom half (softirq, NAPI, tasklet) does the heavy work with interrupts enabled. You see it as si in top.
  • Fault: synchronous. A page fault on a valid but unmapped page (lazy allocation, COW, swapped out) is repaired and the instruction re-run. An invalid access becomes SIGSEGV.
  • Trap: deliberate, such as syscall or a breakpoint (int3).
Timer interrupt -> kernel entry -> scheduler tick: slice used up? -> yes: pick next task, return to it

The tick rate is CONFIG_HZ (250 or 1000 are common). Tickless (NO_HZ) kernels skip ticks on idle cores to save power.

grep -E 'intr|ctxt' /proc/stat    # cumulative interrupts, context switches
cat /proc/interrupts | head       # per-CPU counts by device

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Only syscalls enter the kernel."
  • Thinking a non-preemptive kernel could break out of a loop; without a timer tick it could not.
  • Doing heavy work in an interrupt handler (in a driver), starving everything else.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Difference between an interrupt and an exception? -> Asynchronous from hardware vs synchronous caused by the running instruction.
  2. What is a page fault, is it an error? -> Often a normal event (first touch, COW, swap-in); only unresolvable ones kill the process.
  3. A core shows 100% si. What now? -> One NIC queue is bound to that core; spread with RSS multi-queue, irqbalance, or RPS/RFS, and check packet rate.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: knows interrupts exist. Senior: ties timer ticks to preemption, top and bottom halves to si, and knows tickless and IRQ affinity as tuning levers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A single-queue virtual NIC saturated one core with softirq at 400k pps while 15 other cores idled; enabling multiqueue fixed throughput.

questions.contextHtml:
An API service on an 8-core VM has p95 up from 40 ms to 300 ms after a deploy that moved from 50 to 800 worker threads. Traffic is unchanged at 1,200 rps. Dashboards show CPU at 85%. top and vmstat:

%Cpu(s): 18.0 us, 47.0 sy,  0.0 ni, 31.0 id,  1.5 wa,  0.0 hi,  2.5 si,  0.0 st
procs -----------cpu------ -system--
 r  b   us sy id wa st    in    cs
24  0   18 47 31  1  0  9000 310000

The team suspects the new JSON library (red herring) because it was upgraded in the same release. GC logs look normal.
questions.promptHtml: What does this output say, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "CPU is 85%, scale out" or "revert the JSON library". It ignores that user time is only 18% and system time 47%.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exactly changed besides the thread count? Is the load shared with other processes? Are the threads CPU-bound or blocked on locks? Is st zero (it is, so no noisy neighbour)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll the thread pool back to its old size (a config flag), which cuts the cause without touching the library.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) too many threads: context switch storm (cs 310k/s) and lock handoff in kernel; (b) syscall-heavy path (small writes, logging); (c) network stack work (but si only 2.5%); (d) JSON library (user time is only 18%, so unlikely).
  4. How I'd verify each: pidstat -w -t 1 for per-thread switch counts; strace -c -f -p PID for a short window (or perf trace -s) for the syscall mix, expecting futex dominant; perf top for kernel symbols like futex_wait, schedule.
  5. Root cause: 800 runnable threads on 8 cores (r 24) means constant preemption and futex contention. Time is spent in the kernel scheduling and switching, not running application code, so each request waits longer.
  6. Fix: Short-term: pool back to about 16 to 32 threads for CPU-bound work. Long-term: use async I/O or virtual threads if the work is I/O-bound, sizing by cores x (1 + wait/compute), and bound queues for backpressure.
  7. Prevention: Alert on cs and sy ratio, load-test every pool-size change, review checklist item "why this thread count".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not scale out blindly (still wastes 47% in kernel). Not leave pool unbounded.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if wa were 40%? -> Different story: tasks wait on disk; check iostat -x.
  • What if st were 20%? -> The hypervisor steals CPU; resize or move the instance.
  • Is high sy always bad? -> No; a proxy doing lots of network I/O legitimately has high sy, but the context-switch rate and r tell you if it is thrashing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" timeouts by doubling the pool each week. Throughput fell each time. A graph of cs per second versus pool size made the case to cut it to 24 threads.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reads only the total CPU percent.
  • Hire: identifies high sy plus cs as thread thrash and checks pidstat.
  • Strong hire: ranks hypotheses with evidence, sizes pools by formula, and proposes guardrails.

questions.contextHtml:
An order service on one host has p99 latency of 2.1 s while p50 is 20 ms. CPU is 6%, memory fine, the DB is healthy (query p99 12 ms). Only some requests are slow, about 1 in 40. A short, filtered strace on one worker thread:

$ strace -f -tt -T -e trace=connect,sendto,recvfrom -p 4121
10:02:11.100 connect(9, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(53), sin_addr=inet_addr("10.0.0.2")}, 16) = 0 <0.000030>
10:02:11.101 sendto(9, "\x..."), 40, 0, NULL, 0) = 40 <0.000020>
10:02:13.103 recvfrom(9, "\x...", 512, 0, NULL, NULL) = 80 <2.002100>

A teammate wants to add retries and a bigger HTTP client pool.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries" or "optimise the code". The app code is idle; the time is a 2-second wait inside a DNS lookup.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do all hosts show it or one? How many nameservers in /etc/resolv.conf? Is there a local cache (nscd, systemd-resolved)? Is ndots large in Kubernetes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Point the host at a healthy resolver or add a local cache; reduce the per-attempt timeout for the first nameserver.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) first nameserver dropping UDP packets, resolver waits the default 2 s timeout before trying the second; (b) A+AAAA parallel query conflict; (c) conntrack/UDP race; (d) upstream service slow (strace shows the wait is on port 53, so no).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare timestamps: the recvfrom blocks 2.0021 s, a round constant, a timeout signature. tcpdump -ni any port 53 to see unanswered queries. dig @10.0.0.2 example.com repeated 100 times.
  5. Root cause: The resolver's per-server timeout (2 s default in glibc, timeout: in resolv.conf) is paid on lost packets. The 1-in-40 rate matches packet loss to that server.
  6. Fix: Short-term: fix or replace the bad nameserver; set options timeout:1 attempts:2 rotate. Long-term: cache DNS locally, reuse connections so lookups are rare, enable client-side DNS caching with TTL respect.
  7. Prevention: Metric on DNS lookup latency; alert on p99; load test with resolver failure injection.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not add retries on the request (hides it, multiplies load). Not set timeout below real resolver latency, which causes flapping.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just strace everything? -> Attach slows the target 10x to 100x; filter syscalls and keep it short, or use perf trace or bpftrace.
  • How would you find it without strace? -> eBPF tcplife/gethostlatency from bcc.
  • The JVM caches DNS forever by default in some configs; what then? -> Wrong direction: stale entries after failover (set networkaddress.cache.ttl).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet of services shared one failing resolver. Every p99 graph looked unrelated until a single strace -T showed the same 5.0 s gap (the glibc default for two retries). Fixing resolver health removed every alert at once.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the application.
  • Hire: reads the strace, finds the DNS wait, proposes resolver fixes.
  • Strong hire: recognises the timeout constant as signature, validates with tcpdump, and designs caching and monitoring.

questions.promptHtml: How does strace work, why is it risky on a production process, and what would you use instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the tool's mechanism and cost, not just its flags.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: strace uses ptrace: the kernel stops the tracee at every syscall entry and exit and wakes the tracer, so each syscall costs extra context switches. That can slow the target 10x to 100x. On a latency-critical process I would avoid it, or use a tight -e trace= filter for seconds. I prefer perf trace, or eBPF tools like bpftrace and bcc, which run in the kernel and add little overhead.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
tracee syscall -> kernel stops tracee -> wakes strace -> strace reads regs, prints -> resumes tracee
(twice per syscall: entry and exit)

Flags: -f follows threads and children (without it a JVM shows only the main thread's futex), -T time inside each call, -tt wall-clock timestamps, -c summary, -e trace= filters, -o to a file.

strace -c -f -p 4121                          # summary only; Ctrl-C to see the table
strace -f -T -e trace=connect,sendto -p 4121  # narrow filter
perf trace -p 4121 --duration 5               # only calls slower than 5 ms
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_enter { @[comm] = count(); }'

Newer strace has seccomp-BPF filtering (--seccomp-bpf) that stops only on traced syscalls, which lowers overhead a lot when combined with -e (verify for your version).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Attaching to a hot production process with no filter and causing the outage you were diagnosing.
  • Forgetting -f and drawing wrong conclusions.
  • Forgetting ptrace needs permission (ptrace_scope, container capabilities SYS_PTRACE).
  • Treating -T times as pure kernel time; they include scheduling delay.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does strace -c show epoll_wait taking most time? -> It is idle waiting; wall time inside a blocking call is not CPU cost.
  2. How do you see only slow syscalls? -> perf trace --duration, or bpftrace with a latency histogram.
  3. Can strace see why a thread is stuck in D state? -> No, it is inside a syscall that never returns; use /proc/PID/stack (root) or wchan.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "strace shows system calls". Senior: explains ptrace stops, the overhead and why eBPF is the production-safe path, plus the multi-thread -f trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An engineer ran strace -p on the primary DB's busiest backend during an incident; the stall deepened and a failover triggered.

questions.contextHtml:
A batch-processing fleet of 40 VMs (16 vCPU each) runs the same job. 6 VMs consistently take 2.4x longer than the rest. Same image, same data size. On a slow VM:

%Cpu(s): 41.0 us,  3.0 sy,  0.0 ni,  6.0 id,  0.0 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.0 si, 50.0 st
load average: 15.9, 15.5, 15.2

On a healthy VM st is 0.1. Disks and network look the same everywhere. Someone proposes rewriting the hot loop.
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose and what do you do about it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Profile the code" or "add more VMs". The code is identical; 50% of cycles are going to the hypervisor.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Same instance family and AZ for the slow ones? Burstable instance type with exhausted credits? Dedicated or shared tenancy? Did they start this way or degrade?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop and start (or replace) the 6 slow instances so they land on other hosts, and route work to healthy nodes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) noisy neighbour on the physical host; (b) burstable CPU credits exhausted (cloud throttles, shown as steal); (c) over-committed host; (d) code (ruled out: same binary, healthy VMs fine).
  4. How I'd verify each: st in top/vmstat/mpstat -P ALL 1; cloud console credit balance metric; compare instance IDs and hosts; a fixed CPU microbenchmark across nodes.
  5. Root cause: st is time the hypervisor ran something else while my vCPU was runnable. The guest cannot fix this; it is host contention or a credit limit.
  6. Fix: Short-term: replace the instances. Long-term: use non-burstable types, dedicated tenancy for latency-sensitive batch, and a scheduler that detects steal and blacklists nodes.
  7. Prevention: Alert on st above about 5% sustained; node health check before accepting work; per-node throughput dashboards.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dedicated hosts cost more. Not rewrite code; not raise parallelism (more threads on stolen CPU make it worse).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Load average is 15.9 on 16 vCPUs; is the box saturated? -> Looks full, but half the "busy" is steal, so real capacity is half.
  • Could st appear on bare metal? -> No, it is a virtualisation concept.
  • How does this show in a container on a shared node? -> Different: CPU throttling (cgroup quota) not st; check nr_throttled.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "regression" lasted a week until an engineer plotted per-instance throughput against instance ID. Four hosts had a noisy neighbour; replacing them restored throughput with zero code change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: optimises code.
  • Hire: spots st and replaces instances.
  • Strong hire: distinguishes burst credits from neighbours, adds st alerting and node health gating.

questions.promptHtml: What does a system call cost, where does the cost come from, and how do high-performance systems reduce the number or the price of crossings?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who memorise "syscalls are expensive" from those who can quantify and name concrete mitigations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A trivial syscall like getppid is about 100 to 300 ns versus 1 to 5 ns for a function call, more with Spectre and Meltdown mitigations; I would measure on the target machine. Cost comes from the mode switch, register save, argument validation and cache and TLB disturbance, plus the real work. To cut it, batch (bigger buffers, writev, sendmmsg), use the vDSO for clock_gettime, epoll instead of per-fd polling, io_uring for submission and completion rings, and kernel bypass (DPDK, RDMA) for extreme network cases.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1-byte read/write copy of 1 GB:   2e9 syscalls x 200 ns = 400 s
64 KB buffer:                     32,768 syscalls  = ~7 ms
  • vDSO: the kernel maps a page of code and data into every process. clock_gettime reads the time there with no mode switch (about 20 ns).
  • epoll: one epoll_wait returns many ready fds, versus one syscall per fd with select loops.
  • io_uring (Linux 5.1+): shared ring buffers; you queue many operations and submit with one syscall, or none with SQPOLL (a kernel thread polls the ring, burning a core). Security history means some sandboxes disable it.
  • Kernel bypass: the NIC is mapped into user space; no syscalls for packet I/O, but you lose the kernel network stack.
  • Not all syscalls cost the same: getpid is tiny; fsync can take milliseconds.
# Measure, do not guess
perf stat -e raw_syscalls:sys_enter ./app
strace -c -f ./app

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Optimising syscalls without profiling first.
  • Quoting one number as universal. KPTI, retpoline and virtualisation shift it.
  • Assuming io_uring is always faster; for low rates, epoll plus buffers is fine and simpler.
  • Forgetting that fewer syscalls may add latency (batching delays the first byte).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is clock_gettime fast and gettimeofday in a VM sometimes slow? -> The vDSO needs a stable clocksource (tsc); with some hypervisors it falls back to a real syscall.
  2. Batching vs latency? -> Bound the batch by size and a time limit (for example 64 KB or 1 ms).
  3. How would you decide to adopt io_uring? -> Benchmark with your real I/O mix; check kernel version, seccomp policy, and library maturity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "syscalls are slow so buffer". Senior: gives magnitudes, names the mechanism for each mitigation, and weighs latency and security trade-offs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service calling clock_gettime millions of times per second jumped to high sy after moving to a VM type whose clocksource forced real syscalls; changing the clocksource restored it.

questions.contextHtml:
A UDP ingestion box (16 cores, 25 Gbit NIC) drops packets at 600k packets/s. top shows one core pinned and the rest idle:

%Cpu0 :  1.0 us,  4.0 sy,  0.0 ni,  0.0 id,  0.0 wa,  2.0 hi, 93.0 si
%Cpu1 :  35.0 us, 5.0 sy,  0.0 ni, 58.0 id
...
$ cat /proc/interrupts | grep eth0
 120:  98234112   0  0  0 ... IR-PCI-MSI eth0-TxRx-0
$ ethtool -S eth0 | grep -i drop
 rx_queue_0_drops: 1881233

The app is multithreaded and its CPU use is low. Someone suggests more worker threads.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add workers" or "app is slow". Workers are idle; packets die before they reach the app.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many NIC queues are enabled? Is irqbalance running? Is traffic a few big flows or many (hashing)? Kernel and driver versions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise net.core.netdev_budget and ring size (ethtool -G) to buy headroom; enable RPS to spread softirq to other cores.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) single RX queue, so all packets are handled by core 0; (b) all flows hash to one queue (single 4-tuple source); (c) socket buffer too small (app drops, not NIC); (d) app slow (ruled out by idle workers).
  4. How I'd verify each: ethtool -l eth0 for queue count; /proc/interrupts per-CPU counts; /proc/net/softnet_stat for dropped and time_squeeze; ss -u -a -m for socket drops; ethtool -x for hash settings.
  5. Root cause: One RX queue means one interrupt line and one core runs the NAPI softirq. At 600k pps that core hits 100%, the ring fills and the NIC drops.
  6. Fix: Short-term: ethtool -L eth0 combined 16, spread IRQ affinity (/proc/irq/N/smp_affinity) or RPS. Long-term: SO_REUSEPORT with per-core sockets, bigger rmem, consider XDP for filtering.
ethtool -L eth0 combined 8
for irq in $(grep eth0 /proc/interrupts | cut -d: -f1); do echo $irq; done
cat /proc/net/softnet_stat
  1. Prevention: Alert on si per core, rx_drops, softnet drops. Capacity test at 2x expected pps.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More queues raise cross-core cache traffic; very large rings add latency (bufferbloat). Not add app threads.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• All traffic from one source IP and port; will queues help? -> No, RSS hashes the 4-tuple; use a different hash field or RPS on payload-independent keys, or XDP.
  • Why not raise priority of the softirq thread? -> It is not a throughput problem on one core; parallelism is needed.
  • Where does hi come from? -> Top half of hardware interrupts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cloud migration moved a collector to an instance type with single-queue virtual NICs. Packet loss appeared only above 300k pps and vanished with a larger instance family that had multiple queues.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the app.
  • Hire: identifies one saturated core in si and enables multi-queue or irqbalance.
  • Strong hire: reads softnet_stat and ethtool counters, explains hashing limits, and adds alerts and capacity tests.

questions.contextHtml:
You run a platform where customers upload and run their own code (about 5,000 sandboxes per region, mostly idle, bursts of CPU). Today they run in plain Docker containers on shared hosts. A security audit found a recent Linux kernel local privilege escalation that a container could exploit. Options on the table:

  1. Keep containers, add seccomp and drop capabilities.
  2. gVisor (syscalls intercepted by a user-space kernel).
  3. Firecracker-style microVMs (a guest kernel per sandbox).

Benchmarks: syscall-heavy workloads slow about 2x under gVisor (verify on your workload); microVM boots in about 125 ms with about 5 MB overhead per VM (vendor figure, verify).

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "VMs are always more secure so use VMs" with no cost or workload reasoning, or "containers are fine, we patch quickly".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are tenants mutually untrusted? How syscall-heavy and I/O-heavy are workloads? Cold-start latency target? Do we need GPU or nested features? Compliance requirements?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Patch kernels, tighten seccomp profiles, drop capabilities, enable user namespaces, and read-only root filesystems today. This reduces attack surface for the exploit class now.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The threat is a shared kernel (ring 0). Containers expose about 300+ syscalls to hostile code; gVisor exposes a small set to the host kernel; a microVM exposes a hypervisor interface (smaller and well audited).
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure our workloads: strace -c to see syscall mix; benchmark p99 latency and throughput under gVisor and microVM; measure boot time and density per host.
  5. Root cause of the risk: All containers on a node share the kernel's attack surface, so one kernel bug breaks isolation for everyone. This is the monolithic kernel's cost: a huge trusted computing base in ring 0.
  6. Fix: For untrusted code, microVMs: strongest boundary, pay in memory overhead and boot time. Use gVisor where workloads are compute-bound and syscall-light. Keep trusted internal workloads in hardened containers.
  7. Prevention: Kernel patch SLA, seccomp-by-default, escape-test in CI, separate node pools by trust level, egress controls.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: MicroVMs lose density and add VM management; gVisor can break unusual syscalls and slows I/O. I would not rely on seccomp alone for hostile tenants.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is a hypervisor attack surface smaller than the kernel's? -> Fewer, narrower interfaces (VM exits, virtio devices) versus hundreds of syscalls and drivers.
  • Does a microkernel solve this? -> Reduces the trusted base, but you still need the user-space services and hardware virtualization for tenants.
  • What about memory dedup across VMs? -> It can open side channels; usually disabled for multi-tenant.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A platform moved untrusted workloads to microVMs but kept CI workers on containers. Cold-start p99 rose 80 ms; the team solved it with pre-warmed snapshot pools.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one without trade-offs.
  • Hire: explains shared-kernel risk and recommends microVM or gVisor for untrusted code.
  • Strong hire: segments by trust, measures syscall mix, quantifies costs and has a staged migration.

questions.contextHtml:
A log forwarder works in tests but corrupts data in production when the downstream pipe fills and during deploys (SIGTERM/SIGHUP handlers installed). Code:

void send_all(int fd, const char* p, size_t n) {
    ssize_t w = write(fd, p, n);
    if (w < 0) {
        perror("write");
        return;               // drop and move on
    }
}

ssize_t read_line(int fd, char* buf, size_t cap) {
    ssize_t r = read(fd, buf, cap);
    if (r == 0) return -1;     // EOF
    return r;                  // assume r bytes form one record
}

Symptoms: 1 in about 20,000 records truncated, write: Interrupted system call appears in logs during deploys, and once write: Resource temporarily unavailable when the fd was non-blocking. Another engineer says the code is fine because it works under strace.
questions.promptHtml: List every bug and how you would fix and test them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a retry" without understanding partial writes, or "it works under strace so it is a flaky test".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the fd a pipe, socket or file? Blocking or non-blocking? Are signal handlers installed with SA_RESTART? Is record framing defined (length prefix or newline)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop dropping records on error: add a bounded retry loop in send_all now; alert on write errors.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (the bugs): (a) partial write ignored: write can return less than n on pipes and sockets; (b) EINTR treated as fatal and the record dropped; (c) EAGAIN on non-blocking fd needs poll and retry, not a drop; (d) read returning r bytes is not a record boundary (short reads); (e) read returning -1 is not handled at all.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run under a pipe whose reader sleeps (pv -L) to force partial writes; send kill -HUP in a loop to trigger EINTR; use strace -e trace=write,read to see short counts; unit test with a fake fd that returns 1 byte at a time.
  5. Root cause: The code treats POSIX I/O calls as all-or-nothing. A syscall's contract: returns bytes actually transferred (possibly fewer), -1 with errno for failure, and it can be interrupted by signals.
  6. Fix:
bool send_all(int fd, const char* p, size_t n) {
    while (n > 0) {
        ssize_t w = write(fd, p, n);
        if (w < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) continue;
            if (errno == EAGAIN) { wait_writable(fd); continue; }   // poll(POLLOUT)
            return false;                                            // real error: caller decides
        }
        p += w; n -= w;
    }
    return true;
}

Read side: accumulate into a buffer and split on a delimiter or length prefix; handle r < 0 and EINTR. 7. Prevention: Wrapper helpers used everywhere, fault-injection tests (short I/O, EINTR), a lint ban on raw write for streams, -Wunused-result. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: SA_RESTART fixes some but not all calls (poll and epoll_wait are not restarted); don't rely on it. Not drop data silently.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did it work under strace? -> strace slows the process, changing timing so pipes rarely fill and signals rarely land mid-call.
  • Does a regular file ever do a partial write? -> Yes, on disk full or signal; rarely, so tests miss it.
  • Is writev also partial? -> Yes; loop on the iovec.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A metrics agent lost about 0.005% of samples for months; the cause was a single unhandled EINTR on SIGCHLD from a helper process.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sees only the error path.
  • Hire: finds partial writes and EINTR and writes a loop.
  • Strong hire: covers EAGAIN, framing on reads, fault-injection tests and library-level enforcement.

questions.subtopic: Post-incident review of a strace outage
questions.contextHtml:
Postmortem: payments API p99 rose from 90 ms to 6 s for 11 minutes, error rate hit 34%. Timeline: 14:02 alert on latency (CPU 40%). 14:05 an on-call engineer ran sudo strace -f -p 2210 on the busiest worker (a JVM with 300 threads) without a filter to see "what it is doing". 14:07 latency worsened, the load balancer started marking instances unhealthy, 14:09 retries amplified load 3x. 14:13 strace was killed and recovery began; root cause (a slow upstream) was found later in logs. Output tail at the time:

[pid  2299] futex(0x7f3c..., FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE, 0, NULL <unfinished ...>
[pid  2301] futex(0x7f3c..., FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE, 1) = 0
[pid  2310] write(14, "...", 312) = 312

Management asks whether to ban strace.
questions.promptHtml: Run the review. What went wrong, what are the contributing factors, and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The engineer made a mistake, ban strace." Blames a person and removes a useful tool instead of fixing the system and the runbooks.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did runbooks recommend strace? What safer tools were installed on prod? Was there a canary node to diagnose on? Did the load balancer remove the traced node (cascade)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (Retro) Detach and drain a node rather than debug it live; shift traffic gradually.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (contributing factors): (a) ptrace stops on every syscall of 300 threads made the JVM crawl; (b) health checks failed, shrinking capacity and the remaining nodes took the load; (c) client retries without backoff tripled demand; (d) no safe tooling.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce in staging: strace -f overhead on a loaded JVM; check LB health-check config; review client retry config; check what is on the prod AMI (perf, bpftrace).
  5. Root cause: Diagnosis tooling changed the system under diagnosis, and the system had no load-shedding or retry budgets to absorb it. The real fault (slow upstream) was a 5-minute log search away.
  6. Fix: Runbook: start with metrics, logs and perf top/bpftrace; if strace is needed, use -c with filter for 10 seconds on a drained node. Add retry budgets and jittered backoff, circuit breaker for the upstream.
  7. Prevention: Pre-installed eBPF tools, a "drain and debug" procedure, game day exercises, blameless review with action owners and dates.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not ban strace; it is invaluable on dev, staging and drained nodes. Limit by guidance and tooling, not by prohibition. Do not stop at "human error".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could attaching strace crash the process? -> Rarely, but it can break timeouts and blocking calls (EINTR storms) and slow GC safepoints.
  • Is perf trace free? -> No, but typically far lower overhead; still sample briefly.
  • How do you debug a production issue you cannot reproduce? -> Metrics, structured logs, tracing, eBPF in-kernel aggregation, and a canary node.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a similar event a team kept a "debug replica" taking 1% of mirrored traffic. Invasive tools were allowed only there.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the engineer or the tool.
  • Hire: explains ptrace overhead and cascading effects, proposes safer tools.
  • Strong hire: systemic actions (retry budgets, drain-and-debug, tooling), blameless framing, measurable follow-ups.
